meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'There Are Only Three Great Cities in the U.S.: New York, San Francisco, and Washington. All the Rest Are Cleveland'?
meta.ogDescription: Twain died in 1910. The Cleveland quip's earliest strong match is a September 1975 review in Best Sellers that credits only a Frenchman.

answer.label: Not Mark Twain — origin unknown
answer.authorDates: Earliest strong match 1975 · credited then only to “a Frenchman”
answer.sourceLine: Quote Investigator ↗ found no substantive evidence that Mark Twain ever used this joke — it is absent from the Twain compilations QI checked, including Caroline Thomas Harnsberger’s Mark Twain at Your Fingertips and Barbara Schmidt’s TwainQuotes.com. The earliest strong match QI located is a September 1975 book review in Best Sellers, where the reviewer Edward Gannon credited the line to an unnamed Frenchman he had once heard.

source.excerpt: I once heard a Frenchman say, “There are only three cities in the United States: New York, San Francisco and Washington. All the rest are Cleveland.” (I suggested he add Boston and Atlanta.)
trail: 1910 — O. Henry’s story “A Municipal Report,” in the collection Strictly Business, opens with an epigraph credited to Frank Norris: there are just three big cities in the United States that are “story cities” — New York, New Orleans and, best of the lot, San Francisco. No Cleveland, but the shape of the boast is already fixed (full text at Project Gutenberg ↗).
1936 — a Lincoln, Nebraska newspaper’s answers column names the same trio and credits it to a “Frank Morris.” Still no punchline (Quote Investigator ↗).

1975 — the earliest strong match: Edward Gannon prints the joke, Cleveland and all, in a Best Sellers review, and credits it to an unnamed Frenchman. Quote Investigator verified the page on microfilm (Quote Investigator ↗).

1984 — Mel Leavitt’s Great Characters of New Orleans opens its Tennessee Williams chapter with the “great cities … New Orleans” wording, one year after Williams’s death. That is the form most people now recognise, and the first time any famous name is attached (Quote Investigator ↗).
source.excerptNote: Two details worth noticing. The 1975 text says “three cities,” not “three great cities” — the “great” and the New Orleans substitution belong to later retellings. And the reviewer immediately proposes adding Boston and Atlanta, which suggests that even the man printing it treated the list as a movable feast rather than a fixed saying. Quote Investigator verified this citation on microfilm.

source.rightsNote: No copyright status can honestly be asserted for this line, because no author has been identified for it. Its earliest strong match is a September 1975 book review that credits only an anonymous Frenchman, and a 1975 periodical is in any case far too recent to be public domain in the United States. Treat the wording as of unknown origin rather than as free to reuse.

author.name: Mark Twain
author.kicker: The name it gets pinned on
author.heading: Why the joke lands on Twain
author.bio: Samuel Langhorne Clemens — who wrote as Mark Twain — was born on 30 November 1835 and died on 21 April 1910, sixty-five years before the earliest strong match for this joke that anyone has yet located. He is also the internet’s most dependable magnet for unowned one-liners: Wikiquote’s Twain page ↗ keeps a long Misattributed section for sayings falsely credited to him. This quip is not even in it — the Twain version circulates almost entirely outside the reference works, most visibly after the comedian Russell Brand printed one in 2014.

misattribution.heading: Two famous names, neither of them supported
misattribution.intro: The quip has been hung on at least two celebrated Americans, and in both cases the attribution turns up long after the man was in a position to deny it.

items.why: Quote Investigator ↗ reports no substantive evidence that Twain employed this joke: it is not recorded in Caroline Thomas Harnsberger’s compilation Mark Twain at Your Fingertips, and it is not listed on Barbara Schmidt’s TwainQuotes.com. Twain died in 1910 ↗, sixty-five years before the joke’s earliest strong match. QI’s verdict on the Twain link is a single word: spurious.

The New Orleans version was attached to Williams in Mel Leavitt’s 1984 book Great Characters of New Orleans, which opens its chapter on him with the line. Williams had died in 1983 — QI notes the attribution appeared one year afterwards, and concludes that while he might conceivably have used the joke, it is unlikely he coined it (Quote Investigator ↗).

Brand’s book credits Twain with a version listing New York, New Orleans and San Francisco, hedged with the word “reputedly.” Quote Investigator ↗ calls the attachment improbable. It is the most visible modern printing of the Twain form, and it postdates Twain by more than a century.

A 1936 questions-and-answers column in a Nebraska newspaper attributed the three-cities saying — New York, San Francisco and New Orleans — to someone named Frank Morris; Quote Investigator ↗ records that credit without identifying him and draws no further connection. Separately, and not part of QI’s account, a New Orleans researcher ↗ traces the same three-cities idea to the novelist Frank Norris, whom O. Henry quotes to that effect in the epigraph to “A Municipal Report” (Project Gutenberg ↗). Whether the 1936 “Morris” is a garbling of “Norris” is a guess no source has tested. Neither version carries the Cleveland punchline, so this is an ancestor of the joke rather than an instance of it.

misattribution.truthLine: The three-cities boast is decades older than the Cleveland punchline, and nobody has yet found a name to put on the joke itself: its earliest strong match credits an anonymous Frenchman, and Quote Investigator ↗ leaves the question open for future researchers.

context.heading: A joke with interchangeable parts
lead: The reason this line can be pinned on almost anyone is that it has no fixed text. Quote Investigator’s survey shows the flattering list swapping members freely across the decades — New York, San Francisco, New Orleans, Washington, Boston, Atlanta and Santa Fe have all been named at one time or another — while only the punchline city stays put. A saying with movable parts leaves no fingerprint, so nothing in the wording itself argues for one speaker over another.

The boast came first and the joke was bolted on later. Versions of “there are only three cities in the United States” run back to the 1890s in newspapers, entirely without Cleveland; the Cleveland tag does not appear attached to them until the mid-1970s. That gap is the whole story of the attribution: the sentiment is old and communal, the punchline is recent and anonymous, and the famous names arrive last of all.
detailsBody: 1895 — the actress Vernona Jarbeau tells a San Francisco paper there are only three cities in the United States she would care to live in, and names San Francisco as one of them.
1903 — an Indiana weekly reports a travelling couple repeating the received wisdom that the three great American cities are New York, Chicago and San Francisco.
1912 — at a San Francisco banquet a chamber-of-commerce official jokes that back east they say there are only three cities in the country: New York is one and San Francisco the other two.
1913 — a Cedar City, Utah paper names its own trio: Washington D.C., Salt Lake City and Denver. Everywhere else, it says, is an overgrown town.
1963 — the Associated Press columnist Hal Boyle recalls the version about the only three cities where a man could get a decent meal: New York, New Orleans and San Francisco.

1979 — the AP newsman Hugh A. Mulligan prints an elaborate version in which a visiting student is routed through the colourful cities first and Cleveland last, on the reasoning that everything else is Cleveland. All of these are documented in Quote Investigator’s chronology ↗.
context.pull: The cities keep changing. Only the punchline stays.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator found no substantive evidence that Mark Twain used this joke, notes it is absent from 'Mark Twain at Your Fingertips' and TwainQuotes.com, identifies the earliest strong match as a September 1975 Best Sellers review by Edward Gannon crediting an unnamed Frenchman, records the 1936 'Frank Morris', 1979 Hugh A. Mulligan and 1984 Mel Leavitt / Tennessee Williams citations and the 2014 Russell Brand Twain attribution, and concludes the Twain linkage is spurious.

O. Henry's story 'A Municipal Report', in the collection 'Strictly Business', opens with an epigraph credited to FRANK NORRIS stating there are just three big cities in the United States that are 'story cities' - New York, New Orleans, and best of the lot, San Francisco.

Wikiquote's Mark Twain page carries a Misattributed section for quotes widely associated with him but sourced to another author; this Cleveland quip does not appear anywhere on the page (the only occurrence of 'Cleveland' in the page source is an unrelated reference to the Blaine-Cleveland campaign).
Mark Twain was the pen name of Samuel Langhorne Clemens, born 30 November 1835 and died 21 April 1910.
TwainQuotes.com is Barbara Schmidt's Mark Twain quotations, newspaper collections and related resources site - the sourced Twain quotation directory Quote Investigator checked.

An independent trace of the quote relying on Quote Investigator's 2015 research, rejecting the Mark Twain attribution outright and, following QI, concluding that while Williams conceivably used the joke it is unlikely he coined it.
A New Orleans tour guide's investigation concluding the saying long predates Tennessee Williams, citing Quote Investigator and the O. Henry / Frank Norris 'story cities' line.
O. Henry's collection 'Strictly Business: More Stories of the Four Million' was first published in 1910 by Doubleday, Page & Company and contains the story 'A Municipal Report'.
